This interview happened back in September of 2021, traveling south along the Pacific coast toward Los Angeles.  Steve was rather pleasant to speak with, and giving my first interview right there in the middle of the street was fun.  

I did not find this video link which Steve sent until yesterday! His email was lost in one of my more obscure email accounts. There is no "part two" but there should be someday, so you all can see the precious little things I carry!

Thanks Steve, for reaching out to a stranger traveling along the Pacific Coast Highway.

I recorded this video just prior my departure from my favorite campsite, the one near my favorite hot spring of course,  at the southeastern edge of Imperial Valley in California. 

The campsite appears here exactly as I intentionally left it, one month ago. There is a bunch of stuff as you see, but anything that was important  I  have taken away with me on my bike , or it is buried underground nearby.

All that you see here are things that I found and collected during my 2+ month stay. There are many more treasures you can't see which are buried, ready to be dug up and put to use again upon my return.

Upon departure, I had raked all the grounds and pathways smooth, so when I do return, I will be able to determine if I had any visitors.

The video above shows exactly as I left the campsite, but the photos below show my campsite appeared while I was living and working there.

As humans, we tend to collect and accumulate all sorts of stuff whenever we remain stationary for a while.  We tell ourselves "it can be useful" or that we would like to have it for it's "aesthetic" value. 

What is it that we really need?
My tent, as it appeared while I was living there.

... looking through the main (and only) entrance ... the area is quite wild and the site was overgrown and untouched before I established the campsite.  I worked nearly everyday to clear it out and make the place like home. I built privacy walls all around with the tree and brush cuttings. I even planted a flower garden, but I wasn't able to stay around long enough to watch them germinate.

Needless to say, it is a very nice place to live, especially since it's just a half mile walk to the hot spring ... and just a few hundred yards away, there is abundant fresh water fishing in the All American Canal, which flows north, and is fed by the Colorado River.

... stuff ... as humans, we can't help but accumulate stuff. That's one reason why I enjoy the bicycle nomad lifestyle ... there is only room enough for the essentials, meaning only that which really matters.  What about all the stuff you have collected over time?  How much of it really matters, or is really necessary for your comfort and survival?

For those who have satisfying work, family or spouse to care for, the basic principles remain the same.

... some of the good stuff I found nearby, and collected, which is now buried underground. This cast iron cookware was in very bad condition when I found it alongside a dumpster. It was so bad and corroded with crud, and so heavy too, that I almost left it behind. But I took it, and subsequently found a wire brush, and cleaned them up. Well worth the time and effort, probably a 40 or 50 dollar set.

... all of this stuff I found, free and in the trash.  This is a wasteful, consumeristic society, where it has become easier to just throw things away and buy new again, rather than to take the time and put in the effort to repair, or simply clean things up. 

To me, this sort of behavior is shameful, and should be condemned by all.  One day in the future, this so-called "intelligent" society will pay a dear and heavy price for their ways - ways that are clearly not-sustainable and cannot continue indefinitely.

But as it is now, who cares?  Why it's eat, drink, and be merry, with no concern for tomorrow, except whether or not the 401k is doing okay, or whatever check they have coming in.
Just a couple of days foraging for food in the nearby town of Holtville, seven miles (ten kilometers) away. I buried much of the canned goods to be used upon my return.

Joe Biden sent me money and wanted to let me know. Before this, he sent me 1800 dollars. Well, it's not really money from Joe Biden. The government just creates the money out of thin air. It's called fiat currency.  I trust you all know that because of all this government generosity we are soon going to have hell to pay with inflation. As they say, there is no such thing as something for nothing, unless I suppose if one is a junk collector. I find so much good junk for free everyday, hardly ever need to spend money, so haven't much use for Joe Biden's money, but I will accept it just the same and save it for bicycle and equipment upgrades.
... the stuff I find along the side of the road.  You would be astounded, if you only knew the half of it.

... here is the hotspring again. 

It stay right around 110 degrees F (43 C). A very clean and lovely place, especially after midnight, during a full moon.  I'm really looking forward to returning there ... and hope each of you can visit someday.  The winter months are the best ... and there is my bike in the background.

... things I find and collect, to put in the tree and decorate my campsite. 

Not that I need or care about these things, rather I put them there so that when I am away, anyone who stumbles upon my camp will think and feel that this is someone's home, and that the owner is coming back, and these are his (or her) little treasures.  Now possibly someone may steal or vandalize this stuff, or somehow violate my camp while I am away, but the majority of people who walk this earth are not that way.  

And furthermore, these trinkets are not at all important to me. I place them there as decoys, as I find them in the garbage anyway. 

Just think about it.  What would you do if you stumbled upon a camp like this?  And if you set up your own long term camp, how would you go about it, knowing you have no roof overhead or front door to lock behind you?

Most people would be scared to death to walk near my campsite for fear of snakes and other creatures which lurk in the brush, but really only in their minds.  

For all they know, I am an ax-murderer hiding from the police.

... my tree in perspective.  

Do you have a tree you can call your own?  One that you care for, water, nurture and appreciate? One that shades you during the day, shelters you from the rain and wind, and that you can sleep under at night?  If not, you're really missing out on something wonderful nature has given each and every one of us.

Did you ever stumble upon a beautiful isolated spot in nature, with a tree that someone generations ago must have nurtured and trimmed to create an idyllic setting to set up camp or have a picnic?  

I aim to be that sort of someone who people generations from now will find and appreciate my work, and if they dig deep enough, they will find even more treasures buried beneath the surface.
Every Tuesday morning volunteers empty and power spray the concrete pools at the hot spring.

My favorite time to visit the hot spring is during curfew.  Each morning I awake at 3 am and it's a short bike ride to the spring.  At that time, there is often no one there, but sometimes there is, typically locals, young adults, who are well behaved and often interesting to talk with.  There is no authority watching over the springs, just the unofficial volunteers who clean and take an active role in caring for this wonderful communal asset, an absolute treasure.

Here is an interesting roadside find, just outside of Tucson along Interstate 8 ... it appears a drug dealer was in fear of being arrested by the police and tossed out their drug stash.  Notice a few lighters and crack pipes, along with a scale for weighing drugs, and 13 grams of marijuana buds.

America, where the streets are lined with gold, so it has been said, and it is true. 

So much wealth, abundance, and opportunity, if only people would open their eyes, but they are blinded - blinded by their own selective  media intake, into which they see and believe in an alternate reality, a reality of fear, crime, despair, disease, and evil lurking around every corner of their own neighborhood and beyond. 

So they dutifully lock themselves up in their own homes, surrounding themselves day-in and day-out with their games, gadgets, fictions, food stuffs, puzzles, collectables, entertainment centers, and most importantly, their preferred flavor of media intake, which if mainstream corporate controlled, is vile, ugly, distorted and manipulative.  

And such are their lives, the lives of ordinary everyday people, nearly everyone, the masses, if you will.

For those who see a different reality, for whatever reason, why they are just odd balls, not to be taken seriously, for if they were, the lies would need to be exposed, and that's just too upsetting for most.

We take comfort in our beliefs, whether they be right or wrong, and for all of us, it's so much easier to believe we are right, than to simply accept the fact that, in all that we think we know, we "might" be wrong.

Mobile Technology    
Part One - Introduction

Through the years, I have tested and carried a notebook computer, various brands and sizes of tablets, and both Android and Apple devices. I have not used cellular data services since May of 2018 while in Europe, having decided that cellular services in developed nations are over priced, and not worth the expense.  

You may be one who wants or needs cellular service in your life, and someday I may opt for paying the price US providers demand, given I find a good enough deal for data rates. When that day comes, I will report here on the cost benefits.

At this point, I have decided that the best work-study environment to carry for my needs is an 8 inch Android tablet (model SM-T290), together with a matching bluetooth external keyboard. Your work may require an advanced graphical environment, but for myself, as a Linux System Administrator and perpetual student, I have several work and study applications that I use.

A simple Android table, loaded with the appropriate applications, offers far more suitability and affordable options, along with much more freedom and privacy than any Apple or Microsoft device.

That said, I do carry an Apple iPhone 6S Plus, with the capability of installing a cellular (simm) card, and I will test that combination in the future.  As it is now, adequate cellular data services would be worth no more than 10 or 20 dollar per month at the most, and although that price is possible in some countries throughout the world, it is not possible in the United States.

I do not use proprietary software, that is commercial software, meaning software that is sold for a price, rather I use open-source software, which if I want to upgrade or contribute to the developers, I do so voluntarily.  The software I select and use for my devices is always quite functional and does not include advertising.

As an open-source software user, I am what some may call a "Linux guru."  I don't use Microsoft or Apple products, because they are proprietary, meaning they are commercial, and sold to the public for profit.  As a customer, even though you pay dearly for both the hardware and software, these products do not belong to you, you do not own them, rather you merely lease them for a while, and at the same time, you are subjected to many limitations and privacy concerns.

Therefore, my perspective toward computer technology is different than the majority of mainstream computer users today.  As a "technomad", or what we today call a "digital nomad", I am routinely testing and comparing hardware and software products to determine which is the best to use in every way.

As mentioned, I do carry the proprietary Apple iPhone 6 Plus, but only because it was given to me as a gift.  I keep it on-hand as a backup and for testing purposes. I do not use Apple iCloud services at all, or any of their "pay to play" services.  One day, I may slip a cell card (simm) into the iPhone to test how it performs as a hotspot for data, but for now, I get along fine with only wifi access.

Being limited to wifi access means I have no monthly cellular expense, which is a great saving, but it also means that much of my work and study must be done offline.  To connect to the network via wifi, I must find a free open hotspot, either at Starbucks, WalMart, Target, Safeway, or several other commercial chains throughout America.

Back in the 1970's, I hitchhiked the USA and travelled throughout Mexico. We did not have cellphones, yet we felt secure we would be okay.  But today, not having a phone at your side 24/7 while traveling is probably more than most can tolerate, and if you fall into that catagory, my method of tele-communicating and "keeping in touch" will not work for you.  

As somewhat of a technical expert, simply to have an Android tablet and an occassional wifi signal at my disposal represents far greater computing capacity than the astronauts had when they first landed on the moon.  Add into this mix the potential for cell service and hotspot, and I am carrying with me what would have been considered in my youth to be science fiction fantasy. 

It would do us well if we would each recognize that the power we hold in our hand today is so advanced that it has boggled our mind, yet for most, a smartphone is simply a convenient appliance which we have become dependent upon to always "just work" for us.

I mainly communicate with friends and family through the written word as I am doing now.  I do have the ability to use VoIP, or what is commonly called Voice Over Internet Protocol, Skype or Zoom, but such tools are only really useful in certain circumstances.  

In fact, you can speak to me now by leaving a message at 657-888-5656, but you will need to wait until I connect to wifi to retrieve your message and respond.

But you may ask, what of an emergency?  For some reason of which I am not quite sure, I don't seem to have emergencies.  If I ever do, I am sure there will be some kind soul nearby with a cellphone to call an ambulance. On the other hand, maybe I will just lay there and die like folks did in the old days, before all this technology came to rule over our lives.

Now as a long-time computer tech, I would like to share further about the specific software applications I use on my 8" Android tablet, but that topic will be covered in Part Two.

Socorro County is actually the largest county in New Mexico, with the city of Socorro being the county seat. Socorro is located in the center of New Mexico, and the Rio Grande River runs through county and alongside the east of the city.

My ever evolving
Long Distance Bicycle Touring Philosophy

The right starting point 
begins with preparation and procedure.

Rules for the Road

 - plan to outlive your bike; it will always break down
 - accept with gratitude whatever the road lays before you
 - there are no strangers, only good friends we haven't met
 - make one new friend each day, be it even a squirrel
 - check your bags for stones and redundancies daily
 - accept all forms of hospitality
 - opens doors for future invitations
 - anticipate and move from trouble quickly and strategically
 - time is on your side, so learn to work with it fluently

Humans are fallible,  
all things degradate,
yet we strive to live
in a world where
 - nothing is lost
 - nothing is stolen
 - nothing is forgotten
 - nothing is left behind
 - there are no accidents
 - there are no injuries
 - all that happens is for a purpose
 - we have all that we need

We strive to be
in the right place
at the right time
with the right people
moving at the right speed
headed in the right direction
toward the right destination.

Never hurried, rushed, or anxious
because time will always take us 
where we need to be
regardless how we feel about it.
